items.title: Introducing Agentic AI in Law
items.summary: You receive a 150-page agreement with a request from the client: “Can you review this and tell me what we should push back on before tomorrow’s call?” The work that follows is rarely one task. You check the schedules, compare clauses against your playbook, identify deviations, research an unfamiliar legal issue, assess the risks, suggest revisions and prepare your negotiation notes. AI can already help with each of these tasks. But what if, instead of prompting AI at every step, you could give it the objective and have it coordinate the work from there? That is the shift from AI assistants to Agentic AI: from helping with individual tasks to coordinating the work needed to achieve an outcome. The distinction: An AI assistant performs the task a lawyer asks it to do, one prompt at a time. The lawyer decides what comes next and carries the context forward. An AI agent can take a lawyer-defined objective, coordinate the steps needed to achieve it, adapt as it finds new information, and bring the lawyer in at defined review points. Legal work is a process, not a prompt The legal profession has adopted artificial intelligence faster than many expected. Lawyers now use AI assistants to summarise judgments, draft clauses, explain legal principles, translate documents and prepare correspondence. These tools have already made individual tasks faster. But most legal matters are not a series of isolated tasks. They are connected processes, where the outcome of one step often determines what happens next. A contract review, for example, may involve checking whether the agreement is complete, comparing it against an approved playbook, identifying deviations, assessing legal and commercial risks, researching relevant law and proposing revised language. Litigation follows a similar pattern; reviewing pleadings and annexures, identifying evidence gaps, building a chronology, researching authorities and preparing submissions. Compliance work may involve identifying applicable rules, mapping obligations, reviewing evidence, recording gaps and recommending corrective action. In each case, the work follows a familiar structure, but what happens next depends on what is found along the way . items.title: Calcutta HC pulls up advocate for using slang against judge, asks him to apologise
items.summary: The Calcutta High Court on Wednesday expressed strong displeasure over an advocate allegedly using an objectionable slang during a hearing before a single judge after a plea in which he appeared was rejected [ In Re : Firdous Samim ]. A Division Bench of Acting Chief Justice (ACJ) Tapabrata Chakraborty and Justice Atarup Banerjee held that such conduct by a member of the Bar could not be treated lightly. It expressed concern over the reputational damage caused to the institution by the incident. “Our High Court advocate. It is going all over India, that your High Court, you have these sort of advocates and you people keep silent and don't take any remedial measure,” the Bench observed today. The matter was tied to a hearing from July. The lawyer, Firdous Samim, was accused of using scandalous and unparliamentary language during a hearing on July 23. In a July 30 order, the High Court took suo motu cognisance of the incident and issued notice to Samim to show cause why criminal contempt of court proceedings should not be drawn up against him. "The language used by the said advocate during Court hearing which was being streamed live is an act of misdemeanour and reflects an audacious and contemptuous attitude of the said advocate towards this Hon’ble High Court as well as the Hon’ble Judge presiding over the Bench, in flagrant violation of the Hon’ble Court’s decorum and discipline," observed the Court. The matter was heard today, when the Court observed that Samim was an advocate and not a layperson. “An advocate consciously appears, a prayer is refused and he ends the conversation by using that slang,” added the Court. It also noted that Samim himself was now unwilling to repeat in open court the slang allegedly used by him in July, while at the same time offering an apology for it. “A thing which you cannot utter in any court, how can you seek pardon for that? A thing which you are so ashamed to utter this in court, how can you seek pardon?” said the Court. The Court also rejected a suggestion that the slang was not directed against the judge. The Bench added that the use of the slang may even be interpreted by some as being a comment against all judges of the Court. “(It was) certainly addressed to the judge. items.title: Supreme Court refuses to issue uniform policy against demolition of long-standing properties, asks States to consider
items.summary: The Supreme Court on Wednesday declined to entertain a petition seeking a uniform policy across the country for regularisation and demolition of long-standing unauthorised constructions. A Bench of Chief Justice of India (CJI) Surya Kant , Justice Joymalya Bagchi and Justice V Mohana said such issues essentially fall within the policy domain and thus declined the prayer for constitution a court-empowered committee to formulate uniform guidelines on the subject. The Court noted that circumstances vary from State to State and thus different policy frameworks may be needed to deal with facts of each case. "It would be difficult and may not be prudent for this Court to lay down a uniform policy framework to be applied across various States," the Court said. However, the Court said the States and Union Territories may consider the issues raised in the petition filed by Centre for Law and Good Governance for the purpose of formulating or revisiting their existing policies. "We are hopeful that due consideration shall be given to all such issues by the competent authorities," it said. Justice Joymalya Bagchi, CJI Surya Kant and Justice V Mohana The petition filed by Centre for Law and Good Governance said that settlement and regularisation policies have been introduced in Andhra Pradesh, Telangana and Delhi. However, it added there are cases of unauthorised colonies suddenly being demolished, with or without notice and without any welfare scheme for the rehabilitation of the affected families. The plea argued that demolition, being an extreme and irreversible measure, cannot be carried out without a policy which reconciles the enforcement of planning laws with the rights to shelter, livelihood and dignity guaranteed under Article 21 of the Constitution. The counsel appearing for the petitioner said that different State governments follow inconsistent policies. Demolitions are carried out hurriedly, erratically and unsystematically, the Court was told. "On the one hand, they assure residents that unauthorised structures will be regularised. They collect municipal and property taxes and permit electricity connections. After 30, 40 or 50 years, they suddenly declare the structures illegal and demolish them without considering whether the occupants have any alternative accommodation... items.title: Online Certificate Course on Capital Punishment in India by Project 39A at NLUD - Register Now!
items.summary: Project 39A at National Law University, Delhi (NLUD) is organising a two-month online certificate course pertaining to all aspects of the death penalty as it relates to theory and practice. The course will consist of live, online lectures conducted on the weekends (Sat-Sun) between September 12 and November 1, 2026. It will provide participants with a comprehensive understanding of capital punishment in India, while equipping them with the doctrinal knowledge and practical skills necessary for advisory, litigation, research and policy work in this field. Capital Punishment remains the most severe and irreversible form of punishment which has undergone significant developments, particularly with the enactment of the new criminal law codes. However, structured, practice-oriented training on the subject remains unexplored. Why this Course? Comprehensive coverage: The course covers the theoretical, constitutional, procedural, forensic, comparative and reform dimensions of capital punishment in a single structured programme. Eminent faculty: The course will bring together various eminent national and internationally drawn faculty members, with subject-matter experts in the field of criminal law and renowned legal practitioners as speakers. Doctrine and practice, together: Participants gain both the doctrinal knowledge and the practical skills necessary for advisory, litigation, research and policy work in this field. Hybrid closing session: The course will conclude with a hybrid session delivered by the Executive Director, Project 39A, allowing participants the option to attend either online or in person at NLU, Delhi campus Flexible weekend format: Live sessions on Saturdays and Sundays, designed to accommodate working professionals and students alike. items.title: Supreme Court agrees to hear plea flagging disruption of essential services during protests
items.summary: The Supreme Court on Monday said it will hear a plea flagging disruption of essential services during protests/ strikes. A Bench of Chief Justice of India (CJI) Surya Kant and Justice Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana directed that the plea be tagged with another case concerning venues for protests, rallies and gatherings. "When protests are underway, essential services are disrupted. We do not know who is a protester and who is not. Ingress and egress are completely disturbed," the counsel for the petitioner said. "There is already a case pending before us concerning venues for protests, rallies and similar gatherings. Let this petition be tagged with that matter. But tell us, how can we issue a direction of this nature? We will hear the matter," CJI Kant said. A petition is already pending before the top court over the use of Delhi's Jantar Mantar as a site for protests and gatherings. That plea states that Jantar Mantar is no longer a suitable venue for public protests due to safety and logistical concerns. The plea was filed in the backdrop of the recent student protests that began in June following a call by the online collective Cockroach Janta Party (CJP), demanding the resignation of then Union Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan over repeated question paper leaks. The protests culminated in a "Sansad Chalo" march towards Parliament on July 20. The petition has sought directions to designate an alternative venue for such protests. When that plea was heard on August 3, the Court had asked Solicitor General Tushar Mehta to take instructions on the issue. items.title: Karnataka HC quashes notices issued by police against Cloudnine Hospital after surgery resulted in death
items.summary: The Karnataka High Court recently quashed a series of police notices issued to Cloudnine Hospital and its senior consultant, ruling that an inquiry into a patient's death cannot become a criminal investigation without the registration of a first information report (FIR) [Dr Vinuta B v State of Karnataka] . Justice M Nagaprasanna said that criminal investigation cannot be permitted to disable a functioning healthcare institution. The Court distinguished between an inquiry in an unnatural death report (UDR) and that of investigation after the registration of a cognizable offence. Following procedure, the hospital registered a UDR with the jurisdictional police. Police investigation escalated quickly with 6 notices issued on various dated demanding CCTV footage, patient records, surgical machinery and calling nearly 10 women members of the staff to the police station to record evidence. The hospital issued a representation to the authorities stating that the inquiry had turned into an investigative intrusion. When they did not receive any response to their representation, they approached the High Court. The Court found that the hospital had complied with the police in its investigation and said that the manner in which machinery and equipment were demanded as evidence would obstruct the functioning of the hospital. items.title: Supreme Court moots dedicated afternoon slot to hear long-pending Constitution Bench matters
items.summary: The Supreme Court on Wednesday suggested that it could hold daily two-hour sittings after lunch to take up long-pending seven-judge Constitution Bench references, while reserving the morning or pre-lunch session of the court for hearings in fresh and miscellaneous cases. A discussion on the issue took place before the Bench of Chief Justice of India (CJI) Surya Kant and Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana . The Court noted that there were 29 pending Constitution Bench matters. "There are 29 matters. Some may have become academic, but the legal issue may still survive," CJI Surya Kant observed orally. Justice Joymalya Bagchi, CJI Surya Kant and Justice V Mohana Senior Advocate Kapil Sibal , appearing before the Bench, agreed with this assessment. "The academic issue still remains because there are two contrary views. It will have to be settled," Sibal submitted. "Precisely," replied the CJI. He went on to propose that daily hearings of these matters for a part of the day could help in settling these long-pending cases. "One possibility is to list these matters every day from 2 PM to 4 PM. We can hear them for two hours daily without allowing fresh matters to pile up," CJI Kant said. Sibal suggested an alternative, where the Constitution Bench matters could be heard continuously across three days: Tuesday, Wednesday and Thursday. The CJI flagged a practical difficulty with this approach. "That creates difficulty because routine, miscellaneous and fresh matters cannot then be taken up," he said. Another counsel present added, "The afternoon arrangement would maintain a balance, but restricting the hearing to two hours could prolong it. If heard continuously, Your Lordships can control the time ... If the matters are heard every afternoon, the Bench can continue for four or five days a week while taking fresh matters before lunch ." The CJI indicated the Court could examine these solutions on a trial basis. "Both arrangements have their advantages. We can take up the first matter on a trial basis and see how it progresses. We will have to work it out," he said. items.title: President gives assent to law increasing number of Supreme Court judges from 33 to 37
items.summary: President of India Droupadi Murmu has given her assent to the Supreme Court (Number of Judges) Amendment Act, 2026 , which increases the sanctioned strength of the Supreme Court from 34 to 38 judges, including the Chief Justice of India. The legislation received presidential assent on August 11 and has been notified in the Gazette of India. The law will be deemed to have come into force on May 16, 2026, when the President had promulgated the Supreme Court (Number of Judges) Amendment Ordinance, 2026 . The Act repeals that Ordinance while protecting all actions already taken under it The Bill was introduced in the Lok Sabha by Union Minister of State for Law and Justice Arjun Ram Meghwal on July 20. The Lower House passed it on August 3, following which the Rajya Sabha considered and returned it on August 5. It was certified as a money bill under Article 110 of the Constitution. During the discussion in parliament , Meghwal revealed that Chief Justice of India (CJI) Surya Kant had written to Prime Minister Narendra Modi on May 11 seeking an increase in the Court’s sanctioned strength. The CJI had reportedly pointed to the growing inflow of cases and the difficulty in maintaining the Court’s disposal rate when judges are assigned to Constitution Benches. The recently constituted nine-judge Bench hearing the Sabarimala reference was cited as an example. According to the government, over 92,000 cases were pending before the Supreme Court as of January 1, 2026. During 2025, the Court received 75,410 fresh matters but disposed of a little over 65,000 cases. The government said that the increase in strength would improve judicial capacity, facilitate the constitution of larger Benches and help reduce the backlog. This is the first increase in the Supreme Court’s sanctioned strength since 2019, when parliament raised the number of judges other than the CJI from 30 to 33. The Court began functioning in 1950 with eight judges, including the CJI. Its strength was subsequently increased to 11 in 1956, 14 in 1960, 18 in 1978, 26 in 1986 and 31 in 2009. The Supreme Court currently has three vacancies, with 35 judges serving against its sanctioned strength of 38, including the Chief Justice of India. [Read Notification]

It is difficult to become an arbitration hub if there is no real business taking place in that jurisdiction. London, New York, Singapore, Hong Kong, Paris and Dubai all have considerable commercial activity. Arbitration may become an industry of its own, but it generally develops as a by-product of business occurring in a particular place. India already has that essential element. It is, therefore, easy to imagine disputes arising from Indian business being resolved in India and, over time, supporting an autonomous arbitration industry. However, two issues must be addressed. First, for the world to trust India as a seat, international parties must understand how its courts operate and how supportive they are of arbitration. They must know how courts deal with applications supporting arbitral proceedings and challenges to awards. They must also be confident that there are no parochial peculiarities in the handling of arbitration cases. Second, India relies heavily on ad hoc arbitration. Such proceedings tend to appear less predictable to international parties. A process in which an arbitrator may ultimately be appointed by a court can appear uncertain to a foreign user. Established institutions have defined rules and appointment mechanisms. That makes international parties more comfortable. items.title: The meeting that could have saved everything
items.summary: Between us, we have sat on both sides of the table in commercial disputes more times than either of us cares to count. One of us as external counsel, walking into matters that had already escalated beyond the point of comfortable resolution. The other as General Counsel, sitting inside organisations when the first cracks appeared in a commercial relationship and watching, sometimes helplessly, as those cracks widened into fractures. What we have both observed from opposite sides of the table is the same thing. The disputes that became catastrophic were rarely the ones that started catastrophically. They were the ones that started small, were misread as manageable and were allowed to grow in the silence between meetings that resolved nothing. This is what we want Indian businesses to understand. Not the law of dispute resolution. The reality of it. The pattern It begins with a conversation that does not quite conclude. A joint venture partner who seemed aligned last quarter now seems to be reading the contract differently. An overseas counterpart who once responded to calls within the hour now replies by email, carefully worded, copied to people who were not previously on the chain. A management agreement that ran smoothly for 3 years begins generating questions about data, about fees, about who is responsible for what. Nobody calls it a dispute yet. Calling it a dispute would require doing something about it, which is uncomfortable. So instead, everyone calls it a situation, a misunderstanding, something that will sort itself out at the next meeting. It does not sort itself out. The next meeting produces minutes but no decisions. The same issues appear on the following agenda. Positions that were once flexible begin to harden. And by the time someone finally uses the word dispute, the lawyers have already been quietly briefed, the relationship has already been damaged and the cost of resolution has already multiplied several times beyond what it would have been 6 months earlier. items.title: Every case has a hole. Find yours first.
items.summary: There is a particular silence that falls in a courtroom when the bench asks a question nobody on your team had considered. Every litigator in India knows that silence. You have read the brief four times. Your junior has tabbed the compilation. You have gone over the opening in the car, in the lift, in the corridor outside the court. And then, somewhere in the second paragraph of your submission, a judge looks up from the file and asks one short question that goes directly to the weakest part of your case. You recover. You seek a short accommodation, you offer to address it after the break, you find something in the record. But you know what has happened. The case did not fail. You met your own weakness in front of the bench rather than in your chamber. That moment is what we set out to move. Not to remove it, but to move it earlier. Every good lawyer already knows After years spent around courts, legal data, and the people who practise law, one thing has become clear to me. Lawyers are rarely blind to the weaknesses in their own cases. Ask a competent advocate in an unguarded moment and they will tell you precisely which paragraph of the petition concerns them, which document in the annexures they wish were not on record, which precedent they hope the other side has not read closely. Awareness was never the difficulty. The difficulty is that the awareness remains untested until something forces it into the open, and in litigation that something is usually opposing counsel or the bench, at the least convenient moment available. What a case needs before it reaches court is not agreement. It needs opposition. The role that exists, and the person who often does not The devil's advocate is not a modern invention. It is a formal role of long standing, created for a single purpose: to argue against a proposition so that its weaknesses are exposed before a decision is taken. A role defined not by helpfulness but by resistance. Every serious argument needs one. Very few lawyers have access to one. The reasons are practical. items.title: The future of publishing: From author to authority in the age of AI
items.summary: Publishing has always evolved alongside civilization. From handwritten manuscripts to the printing press, from digital publishing to Artificial Intelligence. Publishing has never been more accessible and becoming an author has never been easier. Becoming an authority, however, remains as difficult as ever. We have spent over three decades working with authors, professionals, experts and leaders enabling, guiding and helping them learn how books influence careers, and help professionals build strong personal brands, credibility, and thought leadership, in an increasingly crowded marketplace. Viewed together, these experiences suggest that the role of books is changing. Books are no longer valued merely because they communicate information. Increasingly, they are valued because they communicate opinion, expertise and trust. That is where a book makes an extraordinary difference. Over the years, we have seen authors receive opportunities they never anticipated, because a book changed how the market perceived them. The book became proof of their expertise before they entered the room. It shortened conversations, built confidence and opened doors that might otherwise would have taken years to unlock. items.title: HC can't grant relief if anticipatory bail plea premature: Supreme Court overturns relief to Sunil Biyani
items.summary: The Supreme Court on Wednesday set aside a Bombay High Court ruling protecting Future Group’s non-executive director Sunil Biyani from arrest in a ₹1,200-crore Goods and Services Tax (GST) scam [ Union of India v. Sunil Biyani ]. Notably, the High Court had granted this protection even though it held that Biyani's anticipatory bail application in the matter was premature, since the GST authorities had not passed any order under Section 69 (power to arrest) of the Central Goods and Services Tax Act. In its February ruling, the High Court had directed that if any such order for Biyani's arrest is issued by the GST authorities, he should not be arrested for a week from the date of intimation of such order. The Central government challenged this ruling before the Supreme Court. It questioned whether High Courts possess inherent jurisdiction to grant interim protection from arrest to a litigant after holding that their anticipatory bail petition is premature and unmaintainable. A Bench of Justices Dipankar Datta and Sheel Nagu today ruled that the manner in which protection from arrest was given by the High Court was impermissible. "We have set aside the direction contained in para 6 (giving interim protection for a week from the date on which any future arrest order maybe passed), saying that it is not permissible in law," said the Bench. Justices Dipankar Datta and Sheel Nagu However, the Court cautioned that the GST authorities must communicate arrest orders clearly, so that anyone facing apprehensions of arrest in GST cases can ascertain which legal remedies they would want to avail. items.title: Rule mandating uniform healthcare rates constitutionally valid: Centre tells Supreme Court
items.summary: The Centre has told the Supreme Court that a rule requiring private hospitals to charge within a government-determined range of rates for medical procedures is constitutionally valid, even as it conceded that the range itself has not yet been finalised due to a lack of consensus among states. The submission came in a counter affidavit filed by the Union Ministry of Health and Family Welfare in response to a petition filed by the All India Ophthalmological Society (petitioner) challenging Rule 9(ii) of the Clinical Establishments (Central Government) Rules, 2012. The rule requires hospitals to charge within a range of rates fixed by the Centre in consultation with States. The petitioner had argued that specialists providing medical procedures in metropolitan cities could not be expected to charge the same rates as those practising in smaller towns and remote areas. The petition first came up before the Supreme Court in April 2024 when a Bench of Justices Sudhanshu Dhulia and Prasanna B Varale had flagged that private hospitals often get land at subsidised rates on the condition that they reserve a share of beds for poorer patients. The Bench noted that hospitals routinely fail to honour this commitment. It had then asked the Centre to respond to the plea. Justice sudhanshu dhulia and Justice prasanna b varale In its response, the Centre defended Rule 9(ii) as a measure rooted in the State’s obligation under Article 47 of the Constitution, to improve public health. It argued that the Clinical Establishments Act, 2010, under which the rule was framed, was enacted precisely because private healthcare in India had remained “largely unregulated and uncontrolled.” The Centre rejected the petitioner’s argument that the rule violated Article 14, of the Constitution by treating unequal patients equally. It clarified that the rule does not prescribe a single uniform price. Instead, it sets a range within which hospitals retain flexibility to set their own charges, based on factors like infrastructure and quality of service. On the challenge under Article 19(1)(g) of the Constitution, the right to carry on any trade or business, the Centre argued that the practice of medicine cannot be treated like an ordinary business. items.title: Hens are 'livestock' under MV Act; owner can claim insurance for loss of hens in road accident: Karnataka HC
items.summary: The Karnataka High Court recently held that hens constitute 'livestock' under the Motor Vehicles Act and therefore, their loss in a road accident can be treated as damage to goods covered by a motor insurance policy [K Veera Narayana Swamy vs Y Yankappa] . Justice Geetha KB rejected Reliance General Insurance Company's argument that hens cannot be considered livestock. It was dealing with the insurer's challenge against the grant of compensation of ₹4.51 lakh by a Motor Accident Claims Tribunal (MACT) to a poultry farm owner after his 2,000 broiler hens died in the road accident. "Livestock means and includes hens. Hence, the hen is considered as livestock" the Court said. It relied upon Section 2(13) of Motor Vehicles Act which states that ‘goods’ include livestock. Justice Geetha KB The poultry farm owner had earlier claimed compensation of ₹5.90 lakh in connection with the death of 2,250 broiler hens that were being transported in an Eicher van. The claimant said the vehicle overturned, resulting in the death of around 2,000 hens, while the remaining 250 were allegedly taken away by people from the neighbouring area. The tribunal awarded ₹4.51 lakh with 7% annual interest. Before the High Court, the insurer contended that the claimant had failed to establish compliance with Rule 74 of the Karnataka Motor Vehicles Rules, 1989 concerning transportation of cattle. It was also argued that hens could not be treated as livestock and that the insurance policy did not cover the goods in question. However, the High Court rejected the insurer's reliance on Rule 74. While the Court acknowledged that explanation to Rule 74 defines “cattle” to include goat, sheep, buffalo, bull, ox, cow, deer, horse, pony, mule, ass, pig and their young ones but not hens, it referred to Section 2(13) of the Motor Vehicles Act, which defines “goods” and includes livestock within its ambit. "In the policy under the head ‘limits of liability’, it is held that the policy is including death of or bodily injury to any person so far as it is necessary to meet the requirements of Motor Vehicles Act and policy i.e. damage to property other than property belonging to the insured or held in trust or in custody of control of the insured up to the limits of ₹7.5 lakhs," it noted. Therefore, the Court held that the claimant was transporting livestock in the offending vehicle and found no reason to interfere with the tribunal's award of ₹4.51 lakh. items.title: Zee Entertainment, Punit Goenka approach SAT against SEBI order barring them from securities market
items.summary: Zee Entertainment Enterprises Ltd (ZEEL) and its chief executive officer (CEO) Punit Goenka have moved the Securities Appellate Tribunal (SAT) against an order of Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI) which barred them from accessing the securities market in connection with an improper disclosure case. [ZEEL, Punit Goenka v. SEBI] The market regulator had passed the order on July 31. It had found that a land parcel in Hyderabad was secretly used by ZEEL to secure loans for promoter-linked entities without board approval or proper disclosure. It barred the company from the securities market for two months and Goenka for 12 months. Both parties, represented by law firm Trilegal, approached SAT on August 10 seeking an urgent stay on the order's operation. The appellate tribunal has scheduled the matter for hearing on August 12. The case stemmed from an unauthorised pledge of ZEEL’s Hyderabad land to secure loans worth ₹726 crore. This were availed by four closely held borrowing companies from lender Indiabulls Housing Finance Ltd (IHFL). ZEEL itself was not a borrower and did not receive any part of the loan proceeds. SEBI's quasi‑judicial authority N Murugan examined whether use of ZEEL’s asset was part of a fraudulent scheme benefiting entities ultimately controlled by ZEEL’s promoter family. After examining the matter, Murugan held that both Goenka, and former chairman and non‑executive director Subhash Chandra were involved in the scheme in which the Hyderabad land was deployed as security for loans availed by promoter‑related entities. This was without authorisation from ZEEL’s board, audit committee or any competent corporate authority. The order concluded that their conduct fell short of the standards of diligence, care, integrity and ethical conduct required of directors of a listed company. The former executives argued that ZEEL ultimately recovered the title deeds, the property was later sold at a profit, causing no loss and no investor harm. SEBI rejected this defence, stressing that securities regulation is concerned with fair disclosure, proper governance and conflicts of interest, not just eventual financial outcomes. Thus, the regulator imposed a penalty of ₹30 lakh on ZEEL and ₹58 lakh on Goenka to be paid within 45 days of the order. They were also barred from accessing securities market for a year. items.summary: The Delhi High Court has asked Supreme Court and High Court judges to share their Permanent Account Number (PAN) and other details with the Income Tax Department (IT Department) to ensure that their tax returns are not processed pending a dispute over taxation of judicial allowances. A Division Bench of Justices Dinesh Mehta and Rajneesh Kumar Gupta passed the order on August 10 an application moved by the Income Tax Department seeking modification of an interim order passed on July 22. The Court directed that if a judge’s tax returns have already been processed and a tax demand has been raised, the demand must be kept in abeyance until the petition is decided. The earlier order had permitted judges opting for the new income-tax regime to declare specified allowances as “receipts not in the nature of income”. The Court had directed that returns filed in this manner should not be processed until further orders. Justice Dinesh Mehta and Justice Rajneesh Kumar Gupta The dispute arose from a September 12, 2025 Office Memorandum issued by the Central Board of Direct Taxes (CBDT) concerning allowances paid to judges. According to the Delhi Tax Bar Association, the memorandum said that judges opting for the new income-tax regime cannot claim the tax benefit relating to rent-free official accommodation, conveyance facilities, sumptuary allowance and leave travel concession. The CBDT’s position was that the new regime provides moderate tax rates without deductions and exemptions. The Association challenged the memorandum before the Delhi High Court. It argued that these allowances are not deductions or exemptions in the conventional sense. Section 22D of the High Court Judges (Salaries and Conditions of Service) Act, 1954 and Section 23D of the Supreme Court Judges (Salaries and Conditions of Service) Act, 1958 specifically exclude them from the computation of salary income, the Association submitted. items.summary: The Delhi High Court recently denied bail to two-time Olympic medallist Sushil Kumar in wrestler Sagar Dhankar's murder case. Justice Purushaindra Kumar Kaurav said that it was a case of "a premeditated and gruesome assault resulting in death" and that a lot of material is yet to be tested at trial. The Court noted that the Supreme Court had raised concerns over Kumar's conduct before his arrest and that "his capacity to influence the outcome of the trial given his standing, have not been shown to have altered in any material particular". "In these circumstances, this Court is not persuaded that the petitioner has made out a case either for a genuine change in circumstances within the meaning of the liberty reserved by the Supreme Court, or, independently, for the grant of regular bail on the ordinary parameters governing Section 439 CrPC/ 483 BNSS. The application is, accordingly, dismissed," Justice Kaurav ordered. [Aniruddha Gaurav Gursal and Anr v. "We find that the order dated 21st July 2026 of the Hon'ble Supreme Court applies to all the Petitioners before us, notwithstanding the shortfall in their attendance," the Court said. It added that the benefit would accrue to even those students who did not approach the Court. "The benefit of the aforesaid one-time protection shall also be extended to other similarly situated students of the College whose academic session was ongoing on 3rd November 2025 and who were prevented from appearing for the relevant examinations during the academic session 2025–26 solely on account of shortage of attendance..." After the Bar Council of India (BCI) challenged the ruling, the Supreme Court stayed it prospectively in May. It then granted a one-time protection on July 21 to students who were mid-session when the Delhi High Court judgment was pronounced. The Bombay High Court said that this protection did not depend on individual attendance percentages and was not limited to final-year students or to Delhi's territorial jurisdiction. "The order dated 21st July 2026 neither confines its operation to students within the territorial jurisdiction of the Delhi High Court nor excludes students studying in States where the concerned High Court had taken a contrary view. Equally, it does not reserve to individual institutions the power to determine whether the one-time protection granted by the Hon’ble Supreme Court should be extended to their students." The College and University must now hold supplementary exams within four weeks, with successful students eligible for admission to the 2026-27 session. items.title: Public institutions must be open to questioning: Supreme Court Justice Vikram Nath
items.summary: Growing awareness of citizens' rights has raised expectations from public institutions, which must remain accountable for the power entrusted to them, Supreme Court Justice Vikram Nath recently said. He further noted that citizens today are more aware of their rights and the institutions that govern them. This makes it necessary for institutions to account for the power entrusted to them, the apex court judge said. “We are living through unprecedented times. People today are far more aware of their rights and of the institutions that govern them. This change was something that was long in coming… But this growing awareness also brings with it a quiet weight. Expectations rise, and rightly so. If citizens are expected to respect institutions, then institutions must be equally willing to account for the power entrusted to them,” said Justice Nath. Institutions must be open to questioning, he added. "That is part of their strength, not a threat to it,” said Justice Nath He was speaking at a lecture organised on August 6 by the Supreme Court Advocates-on-Record Association (SCAORA) on the theme "The Future of Justice Delivery: Innovation, Inclusion and Integrity". The event also featured other speakers including Chief Justice of India (CJI) Surya Kant , Supreme Court Justice V Mohana and Justice Abha Nayar Patel of the Supreme Court of Zambia among others. In his address, Justice Nath also emphasised that the principles of justice must be reflected in the actual experience of people who approach the courts. “Justice, fairness, and transparency cannot remain confined to the language of judgments, speeches, or statutes. They must be felt in the lived experience of those who approach the system,” said Justice Nath. He said this was particularly important in the case of courts, which are often described as guardians of rights. Justice Nath noted that concepts such as liberty and equality acquire real meaning when tested against the experiences of individuals who come before the justice system. He also stressed that the responsibility of ensuring effective justice delivery does not rest with judges alone. Lawyers, court staff and everyone involved in the judicial process contribute to a litigant's experience, he said. Justice Nath further observed that while the values underlying the justice system must be preserved, this did not mean that courts should continue following every traditional method of functioning. items.summary: A United States court has dismissed securities and wire fraud charges against Indian industrialist and billionaire Gautam Adani and two other executives, bringing the criminal proceedings against them to an end. Judge Nicholas G Garaufis of the US District Court for the Eastern District of New York on August 11 accepted the proposal of the US Department of Justice (DOJ) to dismiss all three charges brought against Gautam Adani, Sagar Adani and Vneet Jaain - securities fraud conspiracy, wire fraud conspiracy and securities fraud. However, Judge Garaufis expressed concern about the manner in which the DOJ made the proposal and termed it "highly unusual". " The fact that McCotter came to this decision largely in collaboration with defense counsel, and seemingly without input from the FBI and SEC agents who investigated the alleged misconduct, or the attorneys from the Department, SEC, and U.S. Attorney’s Office who brought the case, appears to be highly unusual, " the order said. The Court's decision to drop charges comes after multiple affidavits were filed by Adani and DOJ over two months. Since Adani was not charged with either conspiracy under Foreign Corrupt Practices Act (FCPA) or obstruction of justice, no criminal charge under this indictment remains pending against him. The Court, however, reserved its decision on DOJ’s request to dismiss the FCPA conspiracy charge against Ranjit Gupta, Cyril Cabanes, Saurabh Agarwal, Deepak Malhotra and Rupesh Agarwal, as well as the obstruction charge against all of them except Gupta. These counts remain open for now because the Department has not adequately supported its reasons for seeking their dismissal. items.title: RGNUL faculty allege misconduct by Vice-Chancellor, give University 48-hour notice to resolve issues
items.summary: Faculty members at Rajiv Gandhi National University of Law (RGNUL), Patiala have given the University a 48-hour notice seeking the Chancellor's intervention in its functioning. In an email sent to Vice-Chancellor (VC) Prof (Dr) Jai S Singh on August 10, the faculty members expressed concern over his recent decision to promote a member of the faculty, which they alleged had overlooked applicable orders and established norms of transparency. The faculty has sought the intervention of RGNUL Chancellor, currently Justice Ashwani Kumar Mishra , Acting Chief Justice of the Punjab and Haryana High Court, or his nominee. Failing this, the faculty said that they would withdraw from routine institutional work and eventually proceed to a "pen-down strike." In the email, the faculty said that new administrative mandates and directions had, over the past couple of years, "increasingly been introduced or implemented without adequate consultation with the concerned stakeholders, without clear institutional rationale, and, in several instances, without adherence to established procedures, precedents or principles of transparency and fairness." This, the faculty said, had created an atmosphere of uncertainty, apprehension and diminishing institutional confidence among them. A meeting between the faculty and the VC, held in the presence of the Deans of Academic Affairs and Research, followed the notice but remained inconclusive. Allegedly, the VC responded to the concerns raised by saying that he would ensure that a fund of nearly ₹1 crore, sanctioned for a Chair under the Ministry of Consumer Affairs, was sent back. This is not the first time Singh's conduct as Vice-Chancellor has drawn scrutiny. In September 2024, RGNUL saw over two weeks of student protests after Singh allegedly entered the girls' hostel without prior notice and made remarks about the residents' clothing. Students at the time also wrote to the Chancellor demanding his resignation . The Punjab State Women's Commission recommended his immediate removal and the Punjab Human Rights Commission filed a complaint over the incident. Even as Singh denied any wrongdoing, the University briefly shut down amid the protests before reopening. He has continued in office since and was nominated by the Central government to the National Legal Services Authority in December 2025. items.title: Muttil tree-felling case: Two accused surrender before Kerala court, get bail
items.summary: Follow TNM's WhatsApp channel for news updates and story links. Two of the three Augustine brothers, key accused in the 2020 Muttil tree-felling case in Wayanad, surrendered before the Chottanikkara Judicial First Class Magistrate Court in Ernakulam on Tuesday, August 11, in a separate cheating case linked to the alleged sale of illegally felled timber. Jose Kutty Augustine and Anto Augustine, the second and third accused in the case, surrendered after the court issued non-bailable warrants against them for failing to appear. Their elder brother and the first accused, Roji Augustine, did not surrender before the court on Tuesday. According to reports, the magistrate court recalled the warrants against Jose Kutty and Anto after they appeared and granted them bail. The court directed all three accused to appear before it for the formal framing of charges. The three brothers are key accused in the 2020 Muttil tree-felling case, in which rosewood trees were allegedly cut down from assigned land in Wayanas. The cheating and fraud case, registered by Ambalamedu Police in Ernakulam, relates to the alleged sale of timber from the trees. According to the prosecution, the brothers allegedly cheated MM Aliyar, proprietor of Malabar Timber Industries, of Rs 1.4 crore. They allegedly collected the money in multiple advance installments after agreeing to sell him 54 pieces of timber. The timber, however, allegedly consisted of protected rosewood and teak that had been illegally cut from the Meppadi Forest Range in Wayanad without the necessary permissions from the Revenue or Forest departments. The FIR was registered against the brothers under Sections 406 (criminal breach of trust) and 420 (cheating) of the Indian Penal Code (IPC). The Kerala High Court later quashed the charge under Section 406, while retaining the cheating charge. In July 2026, the High Court dismissed the brothers’ discharge petitions, allowing the criminal proceeding on the cheating charges to continue. The Augustine brothers also took control of Malayalam news channel Reporter TV in July 2023 and relaunched it. Around the same period, they filed a civil suit before a Bengaluru City Civil Court against Google, Meta, X, and 12 major media outlets, including The News Minute, Asianet News, and Manorama News, over reports concerning the criminal cases against them. items.title: The questions posed by over 500 human remains found at Sri Lanka’s Chemmani mass grave
items.summary: Follow TNM's WhatsApp channel for news updates and story links. A headless human skeleton with both hands bound and held against its chest was reportedly found at the Chemmani-Siththupathi mass grave in Jaffna, Sri Lanka, on Saturday, August 8. The discovery came as the excavation crossed 100 days, with 515 sets of human remains now identified at the site. The scale of the excavation has renewed attention on an allegation that dates back to Sri Lanka’s civil war: that hundreds of Tamil civilians who disappeared after the Sri Lankan military recaptured Jaffna in 1995, were killed and buried in the Chemmani area. The skeleton found last week was, as per a report in the Tamil Guardian, found lying in what appeared to be a normal resting position but without its skull. The neck had been severed, and both hands were bound and placed against the chest. Notably, this is not the first headless set of remains to be found at Chemmani. In earlier excavations, investigators also found remains where the head and body lie separated, including some in which the neck appeared to have been severed. A skeleton that was bound and blindfolded was also recovered from the site during an earlier excavation in 1999. By August 9, a total of 515 sets of human remains have been unearthed at the site, of which 506 have been fully exhumed. The remains include those of children and infants. Around 150 items have also been recovered as evidence by the time the excavation crossed 100 days. But while the excavation has established that hundreds of people were buried at the site, several crucial questions remain unanswered. The people whose remains have been found have not yet been identified, and Sri Lanka’s Criminal Investigation Department (CID) told the Jaffna Magistrate’s Court in July that it had not yet been established whether a crime had taken place. So, what do we know about the mass grave and what could the ongoing excavation establish? How Chemmani became associated with mass graves Chemmani first came under scrutiny in 1998, during the trial of Sri Lankan soldiers accused of the rape and murder of 18-year-old Tamil schoolgirl Krishanthi Kumaraswamy. One of the accused, soldier Somaratne Rajapakse, testified that hundreds of Tamils who had disappeared while in the custody of security forces had been killed and buried in the Chemmani area. items.title: Hyderabad set to get 65-storey Trump Towers luxury apartments
items.summary: Follow TNM's WhatsApp channel for news updates and story links. Two months after Hyderabad named a road after United States president Donald Trump, the city is set to get south India’s first Trump Towers, a 65-storey luxury residential project in the Kokapet area. The Trump Towers are expected to generate a sales value of between Rs 3500 and Rs 4200 crore. Touted to be the largest residential project bearing the President’s name in southern India, the Trump Towers will spread across 4 acres of land and will comprise two 65-storey towers with 2.2 million square feet of built-up area. The project is being developed by Tribeca Developers and Ira Realty and will launch in October 2026. The apartment prices will range between Rs 5 and Rs 18 crore. “Hyderabad is one of India’s most dynamic and rapidly growing cities, and I am confident that Trump Towers Hyderabad will become one of its most iconic addresses,” Trump Organization executive vice president Eric Trump stated. The announcement comes less than two months after the Telangana government named the road in the Nanakramguda area as Donald Trump Avenue. The plaque for the avenue was unveiled by US Ambassador to India Sergio Gor and Telangana Deputy Chief Minister Mallu Bhatti Vikramarka in June 2026. The proposal to name a road after Trump was announced ahead of the Telangana Rising Global Summit held in December 2025. The state government has also announced plans to name a greenfield radial road along the proposed Regional Ring Road (RRR) after industrialist Ratan Tata and another prominent stretch as "Google Street" as part of the same initiative. items.title: NCW’s pre-marital counselling programme in Karnataka leaves key questions unanswered
items.summary: The pre-marital counselling programme recently launched in Karnataka by the National Commission for Women (NCW) aims to be progressive, but leaves troubling gaps. It also raises the larger question of actually encouraging open communication before marriage in a society where such conversations are viewed with suspicion by families. The NCW, on August 10, signed a memorandum of understanding ( MOU ) with the Karnataka government to set up Pre-Marital Communication Centres (PMCCs) at each of the 175 Santwana Kendras run by the state government. The MOU was signed under the NCW’s ‘Tere Mere Sapne’ (Your dreams and mine) initiative. In Kannada, the programme is called ‘Koodi Baalona’, meaning living together. Under the programme, the NCW will provide standardised training modules, train the trainers, and monitor implementation. Training sessions were held across the state in Bengaluru on August 10. Addressing the media, Chairperson of Karnataka State Commission for Women Nagalakshmi Choudhary said that the programme would help young couples discuss issues before their wedding with trained counsellors, aiming to avoid problems in the future. Marriage as a journey One can find instruction manuals about almost everything, but good resources on navigating relationships or marriages in one’s own language are hard to come by. Given that gap, the NCW’s initiative is a welcome step, as it suggests that marriage is a journey, not a goal or destination. It encourages healthy ideas such as establishing mutual communication before marriage and making decisions together. While the programme naturally does not talk about the fundamental lack of agency in Indian marriages, it attempts to orient people towards thinking of marriage and marital relations more holistically. It places emphasis on respect, understanding, and healthy ways of expressing one’s emotions. It suggests acceptable and unacceptable behaviours and assessing one’s work and life balance. One section of the booklet asks the prospective partners to respond to a set of 14 behaviours categorised as red flags (unhealthy behaviours), green flags (healthy behaviour), and yellow flags (scenarios requiring more communication between partners). items.title: Prakash Raj’s allegations ‘not true’, says Bengaluru civic body after voter roll verification
items.summary: The Bengaluru Central City Corporation has said actor Prakash Raj’s name was marked as “Shifted” in the electoral roll after a house-to-house verification found that he no longer resided at the address where he was registered as a voter. In a statement, the civic body said the Booth Level Officer (BLO) concerned conducted an inquiry with neighbours and the property manager at No. 266, Garden Apartment, the address at which Raj was registered. “The BLO conducted an official inquiry with the neighbours and the property manager. It was also confirmed by the owner of the flat through mobile call that actor Prakash Raj is not residing in the said flat from past four years and presently other tenants are residing,” the statement said. Based on these statements, a mahazar, or spot inspection report, was prepared and Raj’s voter status was officially marked as “Shifted”, the civic body said. It added that the property manager reaffirmed the information during a telephone call on August 11, 2026, at 5.30 pm. Jagadish G, Additional District Election Officer (Central) and Commissioner of Bengaluru Central City Corporation, said he subsequently spoke to Raj over the telephone. According to Jagadish, the actor confirmed that he was not residing at the registered address and was currently living at a different address in the Shantinagar Assembly Constituency. “Later, through BLO Form-6 may be processed at the present residing address,” Jagadish said, adding that Raj’s allegations had been “verified and found not true”. The civic body maintained that the action was taken in accordance with the due process of law and statutory guidelines issued by the Election Commission of India. Raj had on Tuesday, August 11, alleged that his name had been removed from Bengaluru’s voter list during the ongoing Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls in Karnataka. His name appeared in the ASDDO category — Absent, Shifted Address, Dead, Duplicate and Others. The actor, who has frequently criticised alleged irregularities in electoral rolls, said he was among the 65 lakh voters whose names had been “deleted”. He also highlighted his long association with the area, saying he was born, raised and educated there and began his theatre career in the constituency. Raj contested the Bangalore Central Lok Sabha constituency as an independent candidate in 2019. items.title: Rape convict and ex-MP Prajwal Revanna found with phone, pen drive in Bengaluru jail
items.summary: Former Janata Dal (Secular) MP Prajwal Revanna, who is serving a life sentence after being convicted in a rape case, was allegedly found using a mobile phone inside Bengaluru’s Parappana Agrahara Central Prison during a surprise search by Central Crime Branch (CCB) officials. According to reports, the phone was allegedly found concealed in Revanna’s clothes. A pen drive and a charger were also recovered from his cell. He reportedly feigned ignorance when questioned about the devices. The recovery has raised questions over alleged VIP treatment and security lapses involving high-profile prisoners inside the prison. Parappana Agrahara police have registered an FIR in connection with the recovery, while an investigation is under way to determine how the prohibited devices reached Revanna. Authorities have suspended Jail Assistant Superintendent Eeranna Rangapur for alleged dereliction of duty. Jail Superintendent Ansuch Kumar has also been served a show-cause notice seeking an explanation for the security lapses in Revanna’s cell. Revanna, the grandson of former Prime Minister H D Deve Gowda and nephew of Union Minister H D Kumaraswamy, was sentenced to life imprisonment last year after being convicted of raping a 48-year-old woman and intimidating her. He was also convicted in connection with the circulation of videos of the sexual assault. The woman, who worked as domestic help at the Revanna family’s farmhouse in Holenarasipura in Hassan district, had alleged that Revanna raped her repeatedly from 2021. He had allegedly recorded the assaults and threatened to release the videos if she spoke about them. Revanna left for Germany after the videos emerged and was subsequently suspended by the JD(S). He lost the 2024 Lok Sabha election and was arrested after returning to India.

items.title: Only half of Telangana cops are trained in new criminal laws, says Home Ministry
items.summary: Follow TNM's WhatsApp channel for news updates and story links. Only half of Telangana’s police officials have been trained in the new criminal laws introduced via the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS). According to data released by the Union government, only 27,747 (52.2%) of the total 53,115 police officers have been trained in the new criminal laws that replaced the earlier Indian Penal Code (IPC). The data was released during the ongoing monsoon session by Minister of State for Union Home Affairs Bandi Sanjay in response to a question posed by Rajya Sabha Leader of Opposition Mallikarjun Kharge. While prosecutors, judicial officers and forensic experts in Telangana have been trained completely in the new laws, several police officials remain untrained. Additionally, only 680 out of 1,110 (61%) prison personnel have been trained in BNS. In comparison, other south Indian states have fared better. Out of 56,773 police officers, Andhra Pradesh has trained 54,764 – a 96.36% rate. Karnataka has trained 44,860 police officials out of 45,324 (98.97%), Kerala has trained 48,623 out of 52,808 (92.07%), and Tamil Nadu has trained 93,075 out of 1,00,970 officials (92.18%). The Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS), the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) and the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) came into force throughout the country with effect from 1 July 2024, replacing earlier criminal laws. While police and matters pertaining to public order are subjects that come under the state list, Bandi Sanjay told the Rajya Sabha that the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP)-led Union government supplemented efforts made by states by providing financial support for augmentation of criminal justice infrastructure under various schemes, including the Inter-Operable Criminal Justice System (ICJS) 2.0, schemes for modernisation of forensic capacities and Nirbhaya fund-supported projects. items.title: Tamil Nadu: Engineering student beaten to death; five students held
items.summary: Follow TNM’s WhatsApp channel for news updates and story links. A 19-year-old engineering student in Coimbatore was allegedly beaten to death by a group of his college mates on Monday, August 10, following allegations that he was involved in an extortion and mobile phone theft incident. Five students have been detained in connection with the death. The deceased, K Amuthan, was a native of Kallakurichi district, studying at Hindustan Engineering College in Coimbatore. According to reports, Amuthan had recently been suspended from the college hostel after allegedly assaulting a cook employed there. He was subsequently staying with friends in a rented room near Othakkalmandapam. On Monday morning, around 5.30 am, a group of masked youths allegedly entered a rented house in Poonga Nagar, where Elavarasan, 18, a second-year civil engineering student at the same college, was staying with his friends. The group allegedly threatened the occupants with a knife, assaulted them and fled after taking two mobile phones. During the incident, Elavarasan and his friends reportedly identified Amuthan as one of the attackers. Elavarasan subsequently lodged a complaint with the Chettipalayam police, following which a case was registered. Around 8.30 am, Amuthan and his friend Sriman, 19, were allegedly intercepted by a group of students near Malmichampatti. The group reportedly identified Amuthan as one of those involved in the earlier incident and took the two students to a ground behind the college. Amuthan was allegedly assaulted there with logs and iron rods. He managed to return to his room around 10 am. However, he developed severe breathing difficulties around 3 pm and was taken to a nearby hospital, where he died while undergoing treatment. Based on Sriman's complaint, the Chettipalayam police registered a murder case. Five college students were detained on Tuesday for questioning, while efforts are underway to identify and trace others allegedly involved in the assault. He claims that information provided by his son was leaked, eventually leading to the attack.
